title: Harambee, "Let Us All Pull Together"
text:
When Kenya became independent in 1963, its new government had far more needs than money. The country's first prime minister and later president, Jomo Kenyatta, called on Kenyans to build the nation themselves, using a Swahili word: harambee, "let us all pull together." It became the national motto and appears on Kenya's coat of arms.

The idea turned into a practice. When a community wanted a school, a clinic, a water supply or a cattle dip, people held a harambee meeting. Neighbors gave money, materials or labor according to their means, local leaders and politicians made larger pledges, and the totals were announced publicly. Families also held harambees to pay a student's school fees abroad or a funeral's costs.

In the first decades of independence, harambee built a large share of Kenya's secondary schools, especially in rural areas, along with many health centers and water projects. These harambee schools allowed thousands of children to continue their education where the state could not yet provide places.

Over time the system also had costs. Politicians used large public donations to win support, contributions sometimes became forced, and some funds went missing. In the 2000s Kenya restricted public officials' role in harambees. But the practice of pooling resources for a common need remains widespread in Kenyan community life.
lesson: Many small contributions pooled openly can build what no single family could afford. Keep such efforts transparent so generosity is not turned into pressure.
source: Philip M. Mbithi and Rasmus Rasmusson, Self Reliance in Kenya: The Case of Harambee (1977); Kenyan government records
caveat: The origin of the word harambee is disputed, and the movement's record is mixed because of political patronage.
